newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Ex-dissident Sharansky hails changes in Russia.
newsitem.headline: Ex-dissident Sharansky hails changes in Russia.

text.p: Natan Sharansky, a former Soviet dissident who is now an Israeli minister, hailed Russia's democratic changes by tasting a new experience on Wednesday -- giving a news conference in Moscow without fear of arrest.

Sharansky was jailed by Soviet authorities for nine years before he was turned over to the West in a dramatic prisoner exchange in 1986. He is back for the first time since then, on a four-day visit as Israel's minister for trade and industry.

His crime, he said, had been to act as spokesman for the dissident and Jewish movements and organise news conferences, sometimes for only a handful of reporters who were willing to defy the authorities and attend.
"After every press conference you knew that you could be arrested immediately, or sometimes you were arrested before the press conference," he told reporters at Interfax news agency.

"To know that I can again be a spokesman at a press conference 24 years after this...and nobody thinking anything will happen to us just because we gave this press conference, is by itself a demonstration that Russia, with all its problems, has made a great step ahead, and that it enjoys freedom."
He added: "I am very glad to think that maybe I also contributed a little bit to it."

Sharansky, formerly Anatoly Shcharansky -- he changed his name after release from prison, was a leading campaigner for Jewish emigration rights and became one of the most prominent political prisoners of the Soviet era after his arrest by the KGB security police in 1977.
His release at the Glienicke Bridge linking West Berlin with Potsdam in East Germany was one of the last Cold War prisoner swaps. He settled in Israel and became a minister last year.
Sharansky said he had enjoyed walking through Moscow's snowy streets. The city looked the same but the mood had changed, he said.

"The country may be the same but the regime is different, the conditions are different. We can all enjoy life in conditions of freedom without self-censorship, conditions of free and, I hope, productive dialogue," he said.
Another good sign, he said, was that the teachers who 20 years ago risked jail or exile for teaching Hebrew were now complaining of more mundane problems such as poor funding.

"The very fact of these complaints showed me the great difference, the great changes that have happened, more than anything else," he said. "After this trip, I look with great optimism on the future of our relations (between Russia and Israel)."
Despite giving the news conference in an open shirt and jacket, Sharansky slipped easily into his role as a minister and avoided making unnecessarily controversial statements.
He said he even had fond memories of his years in prison, including the time he spent at a KGB prison in Moscow before leaving Moscow in 1986 and which he will visit on Thursday.
"They were hard years physically but they were years of a very clear conscience, when it was perfectly clear what was good and evil, where the light and the darkness were," he said.
"It is a remembrance of our common victory because that (communist) regime no longer exists."

Apart from holding talks with Russian government ministers on improving mutual trade, which he says is still far too low, Sharansky said he had plans to meet old friends who joined him in human rights demonstrations in the 1970s.
He visited the grave of human rights campaigner Andrei Sakharov on Tuesday and praised the Nobel Peace Prize laureate. His visit is due to end on Thursday.
